output.headline: Milburn recommends guaranteed path into work, training or education for young people
output.bodyHtml:
Young people would get a guaranteed route into education, training or work under a new youth opportunity service, a year-long review into youth unemployment led by Alan Milburn has recommended – though his call for caution on new workers' rights protections and a slower rise in the minimum wage for young people risks a clash with trade unions and the Labour left.

Under Milburn's plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on the youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person that guaranteed route.

It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.

Alan Milburn published the 278-page results of his review on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a "watershed moment" for young people.

Burnham welcomed Milburn's report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a "comprehensive vision" for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work.

He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver "a new settlement for young people".

"A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government: employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so," Milburn wrote. "That is the give and the get."

Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer's attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.

Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year's rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals. Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review "an opportunity of a generation", adding: "We must change the status quo."

The former prime minister had backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office.

The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people's disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim.

People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are "well established, significant and ongoing".

Related: Milburn's absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone

The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.

Trade unions broadly welcomed Milburn's push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work, though they warned against some of his other proposals.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to "crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full" in the face of lobbying from business groups. "The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people's employment prospects. It's for the birds," he said.

While Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn's recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts.

McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: "We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward."

On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying "caution" when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate.

And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: "There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences. I believe this is likely to be the case."

Business leaders welcomed the recommendations, in particular the call to backtrack on Labour's increase in employer national insurance contributions with a tax cut for under-25s, starting in retail and hospitality.

Maxine Bligh, the interim chief executive of the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, said: "Tackling the Neet [not in education, employment or training] crisis gives ministers the perfect opportunity to reconsider a guaranteed hours gamble that risks costing jobs and damaging the chances of young people accessing the labour market."

Industry chiefs have intensified their lobbying against the government's Employment Rights Act, with bosses finding a warm reception from Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said Labour was pressing ahead with an "unemployment act" that would hit youth jobs. "You cannot solve a youth jobs emergency without jobs, and this government has spent two years destroying them."

Government analysis published this year showed estimated costs to employers could range from £350m to £2.9bn a year, with a central estimate of £1.1bn.

Unions and charities urged Burnham not to water down the plans, arguing that low-paid and insecure work had contributed significantly to Britain's youth jobs crisis.

Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, the shopworkers' union, said "crucial policies" on workers' rights needed to be retained. "We are clear that the government must ensure that employment is fairly paid and secure, with workers being treated with dignity and respect."

Banning zero-hours contracts was a promise at the heart of Labour's election manifesto. Under Starmer, however, elements of the party's plan to "make work pay" were watered down amid opposition from business.

Clare McNeil, the chief executive of the charity Timewise, said: "Where we disagree with Alan Milburn is in any suggestion that the new responsibilities in the Employment Rights Bill will stop employers hiring."

Allies of the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, who had championed the government's zero-hours plan as Starmer's deputy, insisted that her proposals would not discourage employers from hiring young people. However, she is no longer in charge of the policy, which must now be implemented by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.
output.standfirst: A £5.8bn plan funds apprenticeships, training and hiring incentives for young people, with ministers embracing Milburn's recommendation to pay for it through benefit cuts – but his separate proposals on zero-hours contracts, national insurance and the minimum wage risk a clash with unions and the Labour left over workers' rights.
output.progress: Ministers have embraced Milburn's central recommendation to shift funding from benefits into employment support for young people.

output.headline: Ofqual steps up campaign against AI and smartglasses cheating
output.bodyHtml:
England's exam regulator is urging exam boards to train invigilators to spot AI and smart-glasses cheating, and calling for retailers to be barred from marketing exam-cheating devices – though students caught still face “life-altering” penalties.

Ian Bauckham, the head of Ofqual, called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating, and said students who tried to use AI in assessed coursework could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications.

“If you are caught committing malpractice with an important, high-stakes qualification … in extreme cases you can lose the entire qualification which, as I am sure you can imagine, can be life-altering for somebody’s future,” Bauckham told the Press Association.

Related: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says

As coursework submission deadlines near, Ofqual is launching a publicity campaign to make it clear to students that using AI for assessments such as extended essays and failing to declare it will not be tolerated.

Bauckham is also writing to examination boards in England to tell them that exam hall invigilators and supervisors should be trained to spot the “emerging risk” posed by wearable devices during next summer’s exam season.

He said he was increasingly concerned about the potential use of wearable devices during exams, especially those able to access AI.

In a speech to an education conference in Birmingham on Wednesday, Bauckham will say: “It is completely unacceptable for any retailer, online or otherwise, to market items explicitly for the purpose of exam cheating. This has to be challenged.”

Ofqual recorded 2,225 cases of smart device and mobile phone cheating during GCSE, AS and A-levels in the summer 2025 exam season.

Bauckham also suggested that the use of extended essays was under threat because of students’ increased access to AI.

Related: Smartglasses and earpieces may worsen exam cheating in schools, says Ofqual

“We will need a radical rethink of the conditions under which it is done and the design of that coursework to make sure it is secure for the future and remains fit for purpose,” he said.

“Unsupervised extended essays, with no other forms of assessment associated with them … the time for that is likely to be quite short now.”

Academic subjects for GCSE and A-levels in England have had little or no coursework for the past decade, but A-level history and English are among those that still allow extended essays.

Bauckham said: “Where we do have extended writing being completed in unsupervised, uncontrolled conditions that is counting for coursework, counting for qualifications, I want … routes to malpractice, routes to cheating, to be closed down.”

Ofqual recorded 100 cases of plagiarism involving AI misuse in GCSE, AS and A-level entries last summer, an increase from 85 in 2024.

Bauckham said Ofqual was considering ways to guard against AI and plagiarism, including greater interrogation of the sources students use.

“It could mean linking the coursework in some formal way to the examination, whether that’s a written or a spoken examination, to make sure that we have a guarantee that students have genuinely done the work and genuinely understand it,” he said.
output.standfirst: A call for invigilator training, a publicity drive and a bar on retailers marketing cheat devices are part of the regulator's response, after Ofqual recorded 2,225 cases of device cheating last summer and AI-plagiarism cases rose to 100.
output.progress: Ofqual is launching a publicity campaign, telling exam boards invigilators should be trained to spot wearable devices, and urging retailers to stop marketing devices for exam cheating.

output.headline: Mary Peltola makes history as Alaska's first Democratic senator since 2008
output.bodyHtml:
Democrat Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next senator after beating the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, with the result called two weeks on from midterm elections which saw Donald Trump’s party lose ground across the country.

Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.

Related: ‘Aarigaa!’: the triumph of Mary Peltola’s historic US Senate win and what it means for Alaska Natives

“From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,” Peltola said in a statement on Tuesday.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she said. “As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families.”

Alaska was the last Senate race remaining to be called, and with Peltola’s victory, Democrats will control 56 seats in the upper chamber, after winning campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi. The party gained nine Senate seats in the midterms, a sweeping victory that will put them decisively back in the majority beginning next year, when they are expected to embark on an aggressive campaign of both lawmaking and investigating.

Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate.

Peltola faced significant controversy on the campaign trail, after the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit another Republican challenger, also named Dan Sullivan, to appear on the ballot.

Peltola’s campaign had denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run, and after state election officials tried to remove him, Alaska’s supreme court in June ruled he be allowed to appear on the ballot. Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted over the apparent ruse, and Alaska’s top federal prosecutor announced that criminal and civil inquiries were under way, while the state’s governor separately announced plans to open a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme.

Under Alaska’s voting system, the top four candidates from the nonpartisan primary advance to the November general election. Voters then rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives more than 50% on the initial round of counting, the last-place finisher is eliminated and that candidate’s supporters will have their second-choice votes counted.

With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had secured 50.1% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, while the incumbent senator received 45.8%. The other Sullivan had received just 1.7% while 2.1%.

Though Alaska is a Republican stronghold in presidential years, Peltola was viewed as a uniquely potent challenger to Sullivan, a two-term senator first elected in 2014 after defeating a Democrat.

A former state legislator who grew up in small communities along the Kuskokwim River in Alaska’s interior, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022, when she won a special election to replace the longtime Republican at-large congressman Don Young following his sudden death, and became the first Alaska native elected to Congress.

Peltola won a full term later that year, but lost re-election to Republican Nick Begich in 2024

In the race against Sullivan, Peltola’s fortunes appeared to rise as Alaskans grew frustrated with the price increases brought on by Trump’s tariffs and his decision to attack Iran earlier this year.

The state is the largest in the union, and dotted with cities and villages that are disconnected from the road system, and thus particularly hard-hit by the increases in oil prices the war caused. Gas prices in some interior Alaska communities jumped into the double-digits per gallon, while the rise in the price of diesel affected everything from groceries to alcohol, since many communities rely on shipments by sea.

Alaska is nonetheless a right-leaning state heavily reliant on its fishing and oil and gas industries. On the campaign trail, Peltola adopted the slogan “fish, family, freedom” to highlight how she would stand up for the state’s unique interests in Washington DC.

She has cast herself as an advocate for expanding oil production in the state, and addressing the issue of bycatch, or the accidental fishing of unwanted species, which some Alaskans believe is to blame for declining salmon runs.

Late in her campaign, Peltola posted a photograph of herself on Instagram from 1995, wearing the winner’s sash from the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant. “Then and now, Alaska is at the heart of who I am,” she wrote.

Sullivan, meanwhile, stuck to Trump’s side, even as the president’s popularity declined nationwide, and especially in Alaska, according to some surveys. He did not join other vulnerable Republicans in urging an end to the war with Iran, while accusing Peltola of disrespecting voters after a report emerged that she had used a hompohobic slur and abused her staff.
output.standfirst: Peltola's win makes her one of the first two Native American women in the Senate, but the race was dominated by a federal investigation into an alleged scheme to confuse voters with a decoy candidate.
output.progress: Alaska's top federal prosecutor has opened criminal and civil inquiries into the alleged decoy-candidate scheme, and the state's governor has separately announced plans to open a criminal investigation into it.

output.headline: Hundreds of Oxford students rally to honour Jason Arday's memory
output.bodyHtml:
Hundreds of protesters filled the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford, to voice their opposition to an appearance by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described “race realist”.

The event organised by the university’s Reform UK student society – billed as “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: is DEI undermining higher education?” – went ahead on Tuesday evening despite opposition from students, college staff and local politicians concerned that his appearance would create a hostile environment.

Related: Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser

Oriel, which allowed the Reform society to use a lecture theatre, declined to cancel the booking, saying it had a “statutory duty” to allow the blogger and academic to appear.

Earlier this year, Cofnas was the first to raise accusations of plagiarism against Prof Jason Arday.

Arday died weeks later, having resigned from his post as professor at the University of Cambridge, amid sustained media scrutiny which began with Cofnas’s claims.

The crowds outside sought to block the college’s main entrances, with hundreds chanting “Say his name – professor Jason Arday”, while several protesters held signs reading “Remember professor Jason Arday”.

One of the protesters, a first-year student studying English and German, who declined to give her name, said: “I think, given the situation at Cambridge with Jason Arday and given what happened, that we as an institution would be looking to not replicate that in any way or hinting that we could support that notion, [but] acting as an example in opposition.

“I think [Oxford and Cambridge], as two academic institutions, should be working together to banish this from ever happening again. And the fact that we can’t even act as the example, I think, makes me almost ashamed to be a part of this.”

Tommy, a second-year maths student at Oxford, said: “This is not the first of this kind of event. There was Tommy Robinson and the Oxford Union, and obviously there were protests for that as well. So I think it’s quite a nasty pattern that we’re seeing with these Oxford societies pandering to the far right, which is just really dangerous.”

Inside the lecture theatre, Cofnas was asked if he wanted to apologise to Arday’s family, but he declined. He said the implication behind the question was that “we shouldn’t criticise powerful figures”.

Cofnas added: “I would ask the people at Cambridge University who protected him for three years, who suppressed all criticism … I would ask them these questions,” earning a brief round of applause.

About 40 people made it into the venue, with less than a third of the space filled. Protests outside could be heard throughout Cofnas’s talk. At times some members of the audience appeared disengaged, looking at their phones.

Cofnas spent the majority of an hour talking about the history of what he called the “race equality thesis”, and his reasons for questioning it.

He has previously written that black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment” under a meritocratic system.

Anneliese Dodds, the MP for Oxford East, said she had contacted Oriel College after receiving complaints from constituents.

Dodds said: “Cofnas’ views are both repellent and contrary to the facts. Many of my student constituents have therefore contacted me to express their concerns about the student reform society choosing to provide him with publicity.

“I have written to Oriel College to ask what they are doing to act on students’ concerns about this meeting, including on safety grounds.”

While the protests were largely peaceful, a group of police appeared towards the end of the event to clear protesters from the entrances.

Hannah, a first-year law student, said that the size of the protest was proof that “even if Oxford won’t listen to us and won’t cancel the event, we’re still going to show up and we’re going to show that we won’t let that decision silence us. And we will still show that we don’t approve of this and we don’t want this type of behaviour here.”

Misan Harriman, the photographer and former chair of trustees of the Southbank Centre, said he attended the protest because he was concerned by the “damaging” rhetoric that Cofnas espoused.

“The university has failed all the students, not just the black students, by having them see this as something that could be remotely seen as part of the course of free speech,” Harriman said.

Additional reporting by Stanley Smith and Beatrix Arnold.
output.standfirst: Hundreds gathered outside Oriel College chanting professor Jason Arday's name, in protest at a talk by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described 'race realist' whose plagiarism claims preceded Arday's death earlier this year.
output.progress: The Oxford East MP Anneliese Dodds has written to Oriel College asking what it is doing to act on students' safety concerns.

output.headline: Hundreds of recruits to fast-track into senior police leadership roles each year
output.bodyHtml:
Hundreds of people will be trained to boost “frankly inadequate” leadership of law enforcement, the home secretary is to say.

Shabana Mahmood will tell police chiefs and leaders at their central London annual conference on Wednesday that standards must improve as she unveils a scheme to train 200 people a year, after a report in June into police leadership found it was at times “staggeringly” poor.

“The conclusions of the Police Leadership Commission were candid and eye-opening. Police leadership is inconsistent and, at times, it is frankly inadequate,” Mahmood will say, according to extracts released by her aides.

“This is the consequence of an earlier failure to invest in the development of future leaders.

“This government will address it … through the launch of a new fast-stream programme which will place hundreds of talented recruits on a path towards superintendent.”

Between 2023 and 2025, the police inspectorate graded two forces as inadequate, 13 as requiring improving and no forces as outstanding for leadership.

Also moving the home secretary to act was that eight serving or former chief constables were under investigation for misconduct across the 43 forces in England and Wales.

Mahmood will also mention that Devon and Cornwall was at one stage paying for three chief constables, with two of them at one point suspended.

The new scheme to recruit future police leaders will be open to people from any job and includes those who are not working in law enforcement.

The aim is to put recruits on a five to 10-year path to the rank of superintendent and “build a deeper and broader pipeline” of future leaders, according to government sources.

New future leaders will not need a degree and Mahmood’s advisers believe the scheme brings a “new focus and scale” to reversing the lack of emerging high-calibre police leaders.

Nick Herbert, co-chair of the leadership commission and a former Tory policing minister, said: “The introduction of a leadership fast stream is a significant step towards putting those recommendations into practice, and it is hugely encouraging to see this progress.

Lord Herbert added: “Effective leadership is fundamental to improving police performance, cutting crime and keeping the public safe. The challenges facing policing demand ambitious reform, and we must build on this momentum to deliver lasting improvements to leadership at every level of the service.”

Former Labour home secretary David Blunkett, co-chair of the Police Leadership Commission, said more changes were needed: “It is important that the introduction of fast-stream progression is not presented in isolation from the commission’s wider recommendations for a comprehensive overhaul of leadership competencies and career progression.

“Fast-track must not be seen as an elite mechanism, but rather as an opportunity, much like in the civil service, for those with the ambition and ability to accelerate their progression through the leadership and management ranks.”

The Home Office said the 27 recommendations from the leadership commission are being considered. They include a new national academy of police leadership, and more money for leadership training, with a current spend of about £4m in a service costing £19bn a year.

The main question on chiefs’ minds is how many of the 43 police forces in England and Wales will be culled as part of the government’s planned radical changes.

Mahmood will not reveal how many big regional forces will be set up. The Guardian understands the still-unpublished review she ordered by Bernard Hogan-Howe recommended as few as nine.

But the home secretary’s speech will stress that local policing units will deal with everyday crimes if the changes go through, according to sources.

Police leaders have claimed a lack of money has put forces under strain.

Figures show that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding since March led to a 13% increase in arrests for breach of bail and an 8% increase in arrests so people can be returned to jail, compared with last year.

Police estimate this will cost forces £500m by March next year and fear the figure may rise.
output.standfirst: Shabana Mahmood is launching a scheme to train 200 potential police leaders a year, after a commission found force leadership ‘at times frankly inadequate’, with two forces rated inadequate and eight chief constables under investigation.
output.progress: The home secretary is putting 200 recruits a year through a new fast-stream path to superintendent rank, welcomed by one co-chair as 'hugely encouraging'.

output.headline: US charges man over alleged sabotage of military plane in Ireland
output.bodyHtml:
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said.

Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks.

O’Corrain is charged with destruction of US government property in connection with the incident in April at Shannon airport in the west of Ireland, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan.

He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled, the AP news agency reported. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.

The $60m (£45m) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules, which had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and will not fly again, US prosecutors said.

O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged with causing criminal damage and trespassing.

Manhattan US attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on US military assets – and thus our national security – will not be tolerated.”

An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends said he disarmed the C-130 in protest against the US’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza.

O’Corrain plotted the attack on 11 April for months, US prosecutors said.

He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking on to the airport’s grounds, prosecutors allege.

O’Corrain subscribed to a phone app that provided live flight tracking and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, prosecutors added.

He is also accused of trying to contact someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon airport, prosecutors said.

O’Corrain breached the airport’s perimeter at about 4.40 am and broke into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.

The document added he used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed.

He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and put ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.

James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said: “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism.”
output.standfirst: Daithi O'Corrain faces up to 10 years in prison after being indicted for allegedly disabling a $60m US military plane at Shannon airport, which supporters say was a protest against the Iran and Gaza wars.
output.progress: US prosecutors have charged O'Corrain with destruction of government property, and the case is now proceeding through the courts in New York.

output.headline: Trump's $10bn lawsuit against the BBC set for May 2027 trial
output.bodyHtml:
A federal judge has set Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC on course for a trial in May 2027, granting the president a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in the case.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.

Related: Trump nominates Chris LaNeve as army chief after Hegseth fired predecessor

Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.

According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.

“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”

The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.

While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.

In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.

Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”
output.standfirst: A federal judge has set a 3 May 2027 trial date for Trump's $10bn defamation case against the BBC, after extending his deposition deadline to 22 January, having missed an agreed October date.
output.progress: The case is moving towards trial after the judge refused to dismiss it and rejected Trump's own legal arguments against the BBC.

output.headline: Jeff Bezos reveals how he picked Robert Pattinson as new Bond
output.bodyHtml:
Amazon’s founder and billionaire chairman Jeff Bezos has said he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Amazon paid more than $1bn for “creative control” of the Bond franchise last year, striking a deal with the longtime heirs and stewards of the films, shocking fans who worried that Bezos’ takeover would signal an end to the franchise as they knew it.

Bezos said he felt there was “something special” about Pattinson, revealing during an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event that he reviewed several rounds of auditions.

“There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists,” he said. “We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”

He added that he and the film’s director, Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, were initially biased against Pattinson, seeking an unknown talent. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond,” he said.

Pattinson, 40, made his big-screen debut in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire ⁠in 2005 and has gone on to star in ​films including The Twilight ​Saga, The Lost City of ​Z and Tenet.

Related: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians

Bezos’ Amazon acquired the MGM studio in an $8.5bn purchase in 2022. Bond fans and film critics have speculated over where Amazon will take the Bond franchise, with industry experts speculating the company may seek to expand the films into a Marvel-style universe of spinoffs.

Amazon has grown into a massive conglomerate in recent years, which includes not only an entertainment arm, but also computing and the company’s original business of online sales. Bezos also separately founded the space exploration company Blue Origin.

Amazon’s surveillance technology has come under criticism as a Guardian investigation this week unveiled that Israel was using its facial recognition tool to surveil Palestinians as part of a larger project to move its data on to Amazon servers.
output.standfirst: Amazon's billionaire founder says he was 'heavily involved' in casting, reviewing final screen tests with the director, Denis Villeneuve, before concluding Pattinson was 'obviously' James Bond.
